requests.what: Merge the `owned` array above into docs/invariants-owned.json. Every id already has a green owning test on this branch; the coverage map simply cannot see them from here.

EC-SCH-11 calls `max_new_items_per_local_day = 40` and `min_hours_between_introduction_and_production = 4` SHARED constants, and the economy config is the one table. They are currently declared as `DEFAULT_SCHEDULER_ECONOMY` in packages/core/src/scheduler/config.ts, injected through a `SchedulerEconomy` parameter that every call site already takes. Move the two values into the economy table and delete `DEFAULT_SCHEDULER_ECONOMY`; no call site changes.

`ItemId` and `SessionId` are re-declared in packages/core/src/scheduler/types.ts with the SAME brand strings, because the shared type surface had not landed on origin/main when this branch was cut. Identical brands are structurally identical, so replacing those declarations with a re-export is a no-op. Do it rather than leaving two spellings.

FORWARD-LOOKING, not a live conflict: neither `packages/core/src/economy/` nor `spendDailyRefreshItem` exists on this branch, and this request is what must hold when they do. INV-SCH-05's spent-marker must be ONE marker shared by both surfaces, which is `ReviewPoolDay.spentBy` in packages/core/src/scheduler/pool.ts. A daily-refresh helper that keeps its own `spentItemIds` list will drift from it and the invariant becomes true in each file and false in the app; delegate to `serveItemsFromPool` instead.

`startOfLocalDay(day, zone)` — the inverse of `localDayOf`, used by the 7-local-day report window — lives in packages/core/src/scheduler/holds.ts because `day/` is another task's lane. It is day arithmetic; move it there.

`localDayOf` constructs a fresh `Intl.DateTimeFormat` on every call. Measured 2026-09-11 on this Mac: 200,000 calls take 5,706 ms that way against 115 ms with one formatter reused per zone — 28 us per call against 0.6 us, a factor of 50. It is on the render path (every streak chip, every quest countdown, every day-keyed rule) and it dominates every zone-keyed property in the suite, this task's included. Cache one formatter per `timeZone` in a module-level Map; the function stays pure.

EC-PACK-55 requires the Score chip to clamp to THE PACK'S declared ceiling ('a chip reading `29 / 160`' for a completed A1-band Japanese beta pack). The manifest does not carry a declared ceiling yet, so packages/core/src/scheduler/config.ts declares `SCORE_SCALE_MAX = 160` (the corpus scale: blog.duolingo.com/duolingo-score 2024-10-23 via deep/04:147 and deep/02:98) plus an injected `PackScoreCeiling` with `DEFAULT_PACK_SCORE_CEILING = { declaredScoreCeiling: 160 }`, the same shape as `SchedulerEconomy`. Add `declared_score_ceiling` to the manifest, pass it through `displayedScore(state, { packCeiling })`, and delete the default. The scale (the chip's denominator, 160) stays a constant; only the ceiling (the numerator's clamp) is per pack.

WHICH `score_floor` WINS. There is exactly one `score_floor` in the plan's data model and it is yours: EC-PTH-09 / INV-PATH-06 define it as the floor of the target section's CEFR band, seeded by a passed jump-here or placement test, 'stored apart from mastery and never read back by FSRS as evidence of it'. An earlier draft of packages/core/src/scheduler/score.ts had a SECOND field of that name holding the highest chip value mastery had ever earned, with the same `max(floor, earned)` formula, which would have merged silently and then destroyed one of the two numbers. It is now `ScoreState.masteryHighWaterPoints` and is scheduler-owned. Yours is passed IN, never stored here: `displayedScore(state, { bandFloorPoints })`. The display rule with all three terms is `min(pack_ceiling, max(earned, band_floor, mastery_high_water))`, implemented and tested in score.ts; INV-PATH-06's own clause (`displayed_score = max(score_earned, score_floor)`, floor non-decreasing) is the middle of it.

Expose the monotonic-clock signal you already derive for EC-STK-02 / INV-DAY-02 ('a `local_day` regression is honoured iff UTC is monotonic AND the zone changed') so the scheduler can consume it. The scheduler's two-sided elapsed clamp stops absurdity but cannot stop a PLAUSIBLY-SIZED forward clock: measured 2026-09-11 (fsrs.test.ts `[INV-SCH-02] a ten-year forward clock ...`), a card at stability 163 answered on a clock set forward ten years reaches 1604.67 unclamped and 1604.45 at the 3,650-day ceiling, so the clamp buys 0.2 there while buying 853 at a century. From inside scheduler/ a forward clock and an honest absence are the same two numbers; telling them apart needs your signal.

TWO THINGS, and the first is a CI-gate flake with a measured root cause.

(1) `Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"`. Reproduced on this branch: two `pnpm test` runs sharing this 12-core Mac both report 21 files / 163 tests PASSED and both exit 1, with 7 and 6 unhandled `Error: [vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"` (scratchpad logs v2-conA.log / v2-conB.log, exits in v2-exits.txt). The cause is WORKER OVERSUBSCRIPTION, not slow tests: vitest sizes its pool from the CPU count, so two concurrent runs put ~24 workers on 12 cores, the main process is starved past birpc's 60 s call timeout, and the run fails after every assertion has already passed. Proof: the SAME two concurrent runs with `--maxWorkers=6` (12 workers on 12 cores) both exit 0 — 21 files, 163 tests, 56.6 s and 56.8 s (v2-mwA.log / v2-mwB.log, v2-mw.txt).

The obvious remedy does not exist: vitest 3.2.7 exposes NO worker-RPC timeout in config. `dist/workers/{threads,forks,vmThreads,vmForks}.js` build their rpc options from `createThreadsRpcOptions`/`createForksRpcOptions` (`dist/chunks/utils.CAioKnHs.js:9`), which pass only `post`/`on`; the only hook `dist/chunks/rpc.-pEldfrD.js` adds is `onTimeoutError`, which throws. So the fix is to stop the oversubscription, in the per-project block where `testTimeout` already lives (a top-level `test.*` key is ignored under inline `projects` — vitest.config.ts records that probe): pin `maxWorkers`, or set `fileParallelism: false`, and record the measurement beside TEST_TIMEOUT_MS. On a one-job ubuntu-latest runner nothing competes and this does not fire; it fires on a developer machine running two suites, which is how it was found.

(2) docs/ci.md records the whole suite at 7.6 s (2026-09-11, pre-P1). Measured on this branch, idle, 12 cores: 22.11 s / 23.16 s / 29.64 s / 28.26 s wall over four consecutive runs, all exit 0, 21 files / 163 tests, ~120 s of test CPU. Re-measure and record it in the commit that merges P1. Do NOT buy it back by lowering PROPERTY_RUNS.

notes: INV-SCH-01's median clause is asserted over NON-LAPSE grade sequences only (`NON_LAPSE = [2, 3, 4]` in fsrs.test.ts), NOT over 'any sequence of 500 reviews' as the registry text reads. This scoping is deliberate and must be stated wherever the claim is made, including to the founder checkpoint: a lapse (`Again`) legitimately shortens the interval — that is what forgetting means — and asserting monotonicity across lapses would require the scheduler to hide a real memory event. The GUARD's own clause (an early review moves neither stability nor due_at) IS asserted over every history, lapses included. Measured 2026-09-11: with the guard removed, non-lapse histories produce up to 28 outright interval decreases and a median decrease in roughly one history in four hundred, so the restricted clause is still falsifiable.

The early-review guard has a STATE precondition: it applies only to cards in ts-fsrs's `Review` state (fsrs.ts `isEarlyReview`). New and Learning cards are scheduled in minutes and are meant to return inside the hour. Relearning is exempt too, which is the arguable one — an item the learner just lapsed can be re-answered inside the hour at full credit until it graduates out of relearning. That is standard FSRS step behaviour and is the right call (a relearning card cannot inflate its interval, only climb back), but 'the guard covers every review' would be false and is not claimed.

INV-SCH-02's `honest-clock bound` is proved by replay rather than estimated, and the replay is STRONGER for backward clocks than for forward ones. It reproduces the adversarial state on a monotone non-negative clock, so for a forward jump it cannot fail by construction; what it does catch is removal of the >= 0 clamp. The two clamps are therefore ALSO asserted literally and directly (effectiveElapsedMs within [0, MAX_HONEST_ELAPSED_MS]; a `negativeElapsed` row whenever raw < 0; an `implausibleElapsed` row whenever raw > the ceiling), and the ten-year forward clock has its own deterministic test with measured numbers. The residual — a forward clock small enough to look like an absence — is not solvable inside this module and is filed against `day/`. The bound it replaced was an ANALYTIC ceiling (the same grade at maximum elapsed) and that was simply wrong: stability is not monotone in elapsed across states and grades, and `[Easy, Again]` falsified it at 8.2956 against a computed ceiling of 3.9056.

`SCORE_MAX = 150` under an `[obs 2026-09-10]` tag appeared in the first draft of config.ts. No such observation exists in the corpus, `[obs]` was not a declared provenance tag, and four corpus lines say 0-160. It is now `SCORE_SCALE_MAX = 160` with its sources, and config.ts records the deletion in place rather than quietly dropping it: a fabricated measurement that survives review is worse than a wrong number that gets argued about.
